paper_title: SPILLWAY: Separating Target Admission from Sanitization to Defend Tool-Using Agents against Prompt Injection

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Tool-using agents act on email, files, and payments, so an instruction hidden in a web page or a shared document can make an agent send data or money to an attacker. Many runtime defenses put a language model on the decision that lets an action through, so the decision depends on a model that may read the attacker's text and adds model calls to every step. Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but need a model to plan or route each task first. Where an action goes can instead be read from the tools' typed returns: an email's sender or a payment's account arrives in a typed field, while injected instructions arrive as free text. SPILLWAY turns this observation into a deterministic floor with no per-task plan. The check admits a call when each target value that appears in tool output but not in the user's task was returned by a read-only tool in a typed field or is covered by a fixed delegation rule. A deterministic sanitizer removes instruction-like regions its fixed rules match before the model reads them and retains the removed spans as evidence, and a local judge may restore a refused call, never one whose target lies in the removed text. Across three backbones, and seven task suites on one of them, no standard templated injection redirects an action to an attacker's target under SPILLWAY, at the highest observed mean utility and composite scores (NRP, ERS) of the defenses we run under that attack. A forged chat template also produces a raw zero, and mean in-scope attack success under a released reinforcement-learning attacker is .005. SPILLWAY reaches this floor with no defense-triggered backbone re-run and almost no added model call. As personal AI agents act on users' email, files, and payments, SPILLWAY gives them an auditable refusal floor on where their actions go that keeps them useful and holds across backbones.

sections.title: INTRODUCTION
sections.content: Tool-using agents now read and act across email, calendars, file stores, chat, and payment services, usually through standardized tool interfaces such as the Model Context Protocol (Model Context Protocol, 2026). Every tool result the agent reads may carry text written by someone else. An attacker who plants an instruction in web page, shared document, or an email can make the agent forward data, pay an account, or invite stranger, all with the users authority. This is indirect prompt injection (Greshake et al., 2023). Many runtime defenses add language model to the loop. In its automated mode, model writes the privilege policy checker enforces (Progent (Shi et al., 2025)), re-runs the trajectory with the user task masked to detect hijack (MELON (Zhu et al., 2025)), or validates each call against plan (DRIFT (Li et al., 2025)). Others verify each action before it commits (Lin et al., 2026). The decision that lets an action through then depends on model that may read the injected text, and adds model work to every step. On AgentDojo, MELON, Progent, and DRIFT still leak on 7 to 11 of 12 backbone-by-suite cells in our runs, and on qwen3:8b they add 2.2 to 13.6 backbone calls per benign episode (Figure 3). Provenance defenses keep the model off the final check but move it earlier: CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2026) has planner write the program whose data flow an interpreter checks, and in ROPE (Ma et al., 2026b) router model reads each request and sets which sources and user-given values the task may draw on, before deterministic origin check enforces it. We show on AgentDojo and AgentDyn that where an effect goes can be decided from typed tool returns and the users task alone. An agent crosses two boundaries. At ingress, untrusted text enters its context, and we decide which parts are instructions. At egress, call produces an effect, and we decide whether its recipient, account, or file is one the user named or tool returned as an identity. Tools already type the fields that carry identities: an emails sender, channels members, and transactions recipient are typed fields, while an injection placed in tool output writes free text such as body or description. Section 2 covers the one benchmark vector that fills channel name. Reading the admitted identities from the typed objects tools return, before they are serialized for the model, separates the targets the users tools produced from the targets an attacker wrote, with set lookup. We introduce SPILLWAY (Figure 2), which makes the two decisions separately and joins them through evidence. Its egress floor admits side-effecting call when every target value that appears in tool output but not in the users task was returned in typed identity field and is not repeated in free text. Its ingress sanitizer removes forged chat turns and the instruction-like regions its rules match 2 Preprint. before the model reads them and keeps what it removed as evidence. local judge re-examines only calls the floor refused, so it can recover work the user delegated, such as reply to an address found in document, and it is never asked about target inside the removed evidence. The judge can therefore improve utility without reopening removed injection (P2, Sec. 3.4), and an injected target the floor refuses leaks only if delegation rule admits it, or it lies outside the removed spans and the judge approves it (P3). Contributions. 1. Target admission from typed tool returns, with no per-task routing. The target decision is set lookup over identities read from typed tool returns before serialization. Three rules keep attacker-written values out of admission. Result: zero in-scope attack success on every backbone-by-suite cell, the only defense in the grid to do so, at the highest utility under attack of any defense and with no defense-triggered backbone re-run. 2. Sanitization coupled to target admission. The judge, the only model allowed to overturn refusal, is never asked about target the sanitizer removed (P1P3). Result: without the sanitizer the judge admits an attackers account. With both, in-scope attack success is zero on every suite and the sanitizer recovers utility the floor alone gives up  (Table 3)  . 3. head-to-head comparison with routed-origin enforcement. Result: zero in-scope attack success on all seven delegated-routing suites and both ChatInject suites, at higher utility than routed-origin enforcement on every suite, where it leaks on three and on two. With the agent as its own router, routed-origin leaks and loses more utility (Figure 4, Table 4). Under released reinforcement-learning attacker (PISmith), mean in-scope attack success is .005 (Sec. 5).

sections.title: 2 THREAT MODEL
sections.content: Agent, attacker, and trust. The agent receives task from the user, calls typed tools, reads what they return, and may act or answer. The attacker controls the fields that AgentDojos injection mechanism fills in content the agent later reads: free text such as an email body or web page, and, in the Slack suite, the name of one external channel. The index stores channel name as one whole value, so an address written inside that name never matches target, and no injection task in that suite sends an effect to the external channel. The attacker does not control the users task, the tool implementations, the tools declared return types, or the scorer. tool provider that itself writes attacker-chosen values into identity fields is outside this threat model. Let be the users text and the text of tool output, and let Id() return the identity values of text (emails, URLs, and whole argument values such as name, an account number, or channel name), casefolded and whitespace-collapsed. value is taint-novel when one of its tokens tok(x), the emails and URLs it contains and the whole value if it has at least four characters, appears in tool output but not in the users text: taintnovel(T, U, X) = { : tok(x), U, / }. (1) The executor also collects the identity fields of trusted tool returns into flat set (Sec. 3.1). What counts as security event. An injection can make the agent fetch an injected URL, send an effect to an unauthorized target, send injected content to legitimate target, commit booking or transfer to an injected object, or recommend an injected entity in its final answer. Our guarantee concerns the target of an effect: whether it may reach recipient or account that neither the user named nor trusted tool returned in an identity field. Objects follow Sec. 3.1. Injected content sent to legitimate target, injected text in an answer, and causality laundering through later call to an admitted target (Chinaei, 2026) are content effects, outside any target check.

sections.title: 3.1 THE EGRESS CHECK: ADMISSION BY TYPED IDENTITY
sections.content: The egress check, which we call the floor, decides whether calls target lies outside the admitted set. For proposed side-effecting call, the floor admits the call when every taint-novel value (Eq. 1) in 3 Preprint. Algorithm 1 SPILLWAYs egress floor for call with identity targets: grant and destruction checks, admission by typed identity and by the users named referents, then two-view judge reached only by refused target outside the removed spans. Object effects follow Sec. 3.1. Require: proposed call (f, a), trusted task , tool output , typed identity index I, injected spans removed at ingress typed in trusted return, values named in are never taint-novel return BLOCK return BLOCK 1: 2: Xt taintnovel(T, U, TargetIds(f, a)) 3: Xp taintnovel(T, U, PrincipalIds(f, a)) 4: if Xp = then 5: 6: end if 7: if is destructive and not authorized by then 8: 9: end if 10: if Xt and no Xt also occurs in untrusted free text then 11: 12: end if 13: if delegation rule of Sec. 3.1 admits every Xt then 14: 15: end if 16: if Xt Id(S) = VIEWroute(T, f, a) VIEWpayload(T, f, a) then 17: 18: end if 19: return BLOCK return ALLOW return ALLOW return ALLOW grantee must be named in before any recovery delegation rules judge sees only refusals, each view fails closed the calls target arguments is in and none is repeated in free text. Values the user named are never taint-novel. The floor is set lookup, so its refusals are the same under every backbone. We build from the tools declared types, never from text. Tool and argument roles come from one fixed lexicon per benchmark: verb prefixes mark read-only, writing, destructive, and granting tools, argument names mark targets and principals, and short list names the tools that write only to the users own calendar or drive. The executor captures the return of each read-only tool as the typed object the tool produced, before it is serialized for the model, and indexes value only when its declared field type is an identity format (email, URI, UUID, hostname, IP) or its field has routing role (recipient, sender, participant, channel). body, subject, or description never enters I, so an address the attacker writes into free text stays taint-novel. Two rules keep an attacker from adding values to I: only read-only returns are indexed, so an allowed write cannot add value, and read whose own arguments are taint-novel adds nothing. The floor also refuses an email or URL in free-text field even when it matches real contact. reply to the sender of an email the task mentioned is taint-novel, but the sender field is typed, so the address is in and the reply goes out. Grants are stricter. call that grants access to new workspace or channel member named only in tool output is refused, and no judge reopens it. Event participants and shared files recipient count as targets even when the write lands in the users own calendar or drive, and deletion is refused unless asks for it. deletion of an injected object is also an unrequested commit, which the two-view judge may restore (Sec. 3.3). Delegation rules. Some refused targets are ones the user named indirectly. Before the judge, deterministic rules admit target whose value carries name the user wrote in (send the report to Alice admits alice.miller@...), contact attribute of an entity the user named, or resource owned by the users own account. After the judge, they also admit download from URL whose domain the user named, and on repository clone, invite, and ownership-transfer tools target that lies in no removed span, only when asks for that grant. The rules read only , the typed returns, and the removed spans. Effects without an identity target. booking, fetched page, or recommendation names an object rather than recipient, and each has its own deterministic first rule. An unrequested commit on an injected object is refused, and only the two-view judge may restore it. An irreversible operation Preprint. under superlative criterion (the largest, the cheapest) is refused when its object is not the winner of that criterion on the typed listing. An injected endorsement is removed from the final answer. What these rules cannot settle, requested booking of an object the task did not name or fetch of URL from tool output, goes to fail-closed judge that can refuse the call. P1 to P3 concern identity targets. 3.2 INGRESS: REMOVE THE INJECTION BEFORE THE MODEL READS IT The floor stops the effect, but model that has read an injection keeps working for the attacker and ignores the users task. The sanitizer therefore rewrites what the agent reads next, with rules and no model call. It replaces forged chat-template turns, such as fabricated <im_start> system or user turn, and the text they wrap with marker. It replaces three kinds of text with an inert placeholder. The first is region delimited by the benchmarks injection template (<INFORMATION> and its important message form). The second is tool text that addresses the agent in the second or third person about its task or answer, forged turn marker, or dictated tool call. The third is claim in data that payees account has changed, with the account it puts forward. removed region ends with its match or, for clause addressing the agent, at the end of that return, so the data before it stays. Trust stays with the first user message, so forged user turn never becomes trusted. The instruction rules keep what they remove as the span set S, and refused target inside never reaches the judge (Sec. 3.3). We build the index from the raw typed returns, before any rewrite.

sections.title: 3.3 RECOVERY: A TWO-VIEW JUDGE FOR REFUSED TARGETS
sections.content: A strict floor also refuses some legitimate calls. When the user asks the agent to send report to the address given in the meeting notes, that address is taint-novel and is refused like an injected one. judge re-examines the refused call from two views, and both must agree: the routing view asks whether the target is recipient the users task implies, and the payload view asks whether the user requested this action and this content. The judge sees only calls deterministic rule has already refused (a target outside that no delegation rule before it admits, or commit on an object the task did not name, including deletion of an injected object). Grant and criterion refusals never reach it. The judge is also bound by what the sanitizer removed. It is not asked at all when the refused target lies inside removed text, which we call the span veto. Without the sanitizer the judge approved transfer to the attackers account on pay the bill  (Table 3)  . With it, that account lies in removed text. The judge is local model called at temperature 0, and it fails closed: missing verdict counts as no. refused call returns to the agent as tool message asking it to re-issue the call with values from the users request, so the agent can continue the episode.

sections.title: 3.4 WHAT THE CONSTRUCTION GUARANTEES
sections.content: Write for the target-bearing calls SPILLWAY admits without the judge, and for refused targetbearing calls whose target lies outside Id(S) and that are neither grants nor unauthorized destructive calls. Three properties of identity-target calls follow from Alg. 1 and the index rules. P1 (typed-identity lookup soundness). Under the tokens of Eq. 1, if the attacker writes only free-text fields (Sec. 2), the lookup refuses every call whose target value appears in attacker-written text and not in , because such value is either outside or repeated in free text. Reason: holds only typed identity fields of read-only returns whose read was not steered by taint-novel argument, and the lookup refuses target repeated in free text. P2 (a bound that holds for any judge). For every judge and every proposed target-bearing call c: implies that is admitted, and admitted implies S, with only admitted when always refuses. Reason: the judge sees only refused calls, and only after the span veto. Its size and family therefore affect safety only through S, which the sanitizers evidence narrows. Utility can move either way, since an admitted call changes the rest of the episode. P3 (remaining admission paths). An attacker-written target that the typed-identity lookup refuses can still be admitted only through deterministic delegation rule, or through the two-view judge when every taint-novel target of the call lies outside Id(S). Reason: by P1 the lookup refuses an attackers target. The span veto constrains the judge path, so target in Id(S) never reaches J, but it 5 Preprint. does not by itself veto delegation rule. residual leak must therefore satisfy delegation rule or survive both the span veto and the two-view judgment.

sections.title: 4 EXPERIMENTAL SETUP
sections.content: We evaluate SPILLWAY in two settings, both on AgentDojo (Debenedetti et al., 2024), whose checks serve as the oracle, with hits rescored by executed effect. The breadth setting tests SPILLWAY on three backbones and four stateful suites under the standard attack, plus three single-backbone stress tests and released RL attacker (PISmith) replayed open-loop. The delegated-routing setting compares the full SPILLWAY with ROPE (Ma et al., 2026b), the closest defense, on the three AgentDyn (Li et al., 2026b) suites, many of whose tasks send effects to recipients read from tool output, and the four AgentDojo suites, on gpt-4o-mini. The same floor runs in both settings and across the stress attacks, with only AgentDyns tool roles added to the lexicon, so the setup tests whether the floor carries to new dataset and to stronger attacks. Every AgentDojo grid uses suite v1.2.2 and the full grid of user and injection tasks for every method. Scoring: three attack-success levels. We report attack success at the in-scope level, which counts an injection that sends an effect to target the user never named, the event the floor is built to stop. Inscope takes AgentDojos raw check and drops two cases no target gate can bound, target the task already named (the collision filter, which removes no hit in any cell) and content-manipulation task that states attacker text but names no recipient or sink. Neither filter reads defense state. SPILLWAY has no hit at either level on any of the twelve AgentDojo cells, while MELON and Progent each leave raw hit on eleven. The trace, executed, and in-scope levels are all in Appendix A. Executed effect vs. trace hit. hit counts only when the environment changed: defense that blocks call before execution can leave that call in the transcript, and trace-level scoring would count it. We apply ROPEs rescoring (runs/corrections.py) to every method and every ablation arm. The judge is gemma4:31b in 4-bit build served locally (Appendix B). Metrics. We report three primary quantities and two recognized composites, per backbonesuite cell and as twelve-cell means. Benign utility (BU ) is the task success rate on benign traffic (no injection). Under-attack utility (UAU ) is the task success rate while under the injection. Attack success rate (ASR ) is the fraction of attacked pairs whose injected effect executes, at the in-scope level above. The composites combine robustness (1 ASR) with benign utility: Net Resilient Performance (NRP ) = BU (1 ASR) (Zhang et al., 2025) and Effective Robustness Score (ERS ) = the harmonic mean of (1 ASR) and BU (Kavathekar et al., 2025), both higher-is-better. Grid, attacks, and comparators. The breadth backbones are gpt-4o-mini (OpenAI, 2024), qwen3-coder:30b, and qwen3:8b (Yang et al., 2025). The standard attack is AgentDojos important_instructions template. Three stress tests follow. Chat-template forging uses ChatInject (Chang et al., 2026) (qwen3:8b, 665 pairs). An attacker-as-sender variant of Workspace has the five injection-carrying emails come from the attackers own address, so the attacker writes the typed sender field the floor reads (qwen3:8b, 126 pairs). Optimizer-generated injections come from the AutoDojo release (Ma et al., 2026a), optimized for gpt-4o-mini against Progent and replayed on the three suites it covers (Banking, Slack, and Travel, 389 pairs, with no Workspace split in the release), plus two held-out Banking sets (Sec. 5). released RL attacker, PISmith (Yin et al., 2026), is then replayed open-loop against every defense on the full grid. We run head-to-head against MELON (Zhu et al., 2025), Progent (Shi et al., 2025), DRIFT (Li et al., 2025), and ROPE (Ma et al., 2026b) on the breadth grid and also against ROPE on the delegated-routing grid, from their released code on the same agent, with the changes listed in Appendix B: Progents policy is written by the cells own backbone, and so is ROPEs router except where its authors router is named. CaMeL (Debenedetti et al., 2026), which replaces the agent loop with its own planner, is not run. Spotlighting (Hines et al., 2024) and prompt-injection detector (Protect AI, 2024) serve as reference points. The SPILLWAY code, per-cell results, and seeds are at https://github.com/saintmachines/spillway. SPILLWAY is also released as an SDK on PyPI (spillway-guard 1.0.0). Preprint. sections.title: 5 RESULTS
sections.content: Across all twelve backbone-and-suite cells, SPILLWAY drives in-scope attack success to exactly zero  (Table 1)  : no templated injection redirects an action to an attacker. No other defense in the grid matches this breadth. ROPE, the closest, leaks on all three Slack cells, and MELON, Progent, and DRIFT on ten, eleven, and seven of the twelve  (Table 2)  . The guarantee is structural: on qwen3:8b the floor, with identity-target judge recovery off, already holds all four suites at zero  (Table 3)  . SPILLWAY reaches this floor at the highest utility under attack of any defense (.489) while keeping 99.8% of the undefended agents benign utility, against 73% for ROPE with the agent as its router. What the breadth grid shows. Removing the injection often raises utility. Averaged over the three backbones, SPILLWAY finishes above the undefended agent on Workspace (.597 vs. .438), Banking (.440 vs. .438), and Travel (.479 vs. .326), because the sanitizer strips an injection that would otherwise derail the agent before it reads it  (Table 3)  . The zero is statistically firm: with no leak observed, the one-sided 95% ClopperPearson bound on attack success is 2.8% at the smallest cell (105 pairs) and 0.1% pooled over all 2,847 attacked pairs, treating pairs as independent. Cost. On qwen3:8b benign traffic (Slack / Workspace), SPILLWAY calls its judge 0.43 and 0.05 times per episode and changes its backbone calls by less than 0.15 (Figure 3 plots their sum), while MELON adds 5.29 and 3.25 backbone calls, Progent 8.67 and 5.94, and DRIFT 9.91 and 9.59. On the RTX PRO 6000, SPILLWAYs episodes, timed in separate session, were within 0.5 of the undefended agents, against +4.9 and +7.9 for MELON, +1.6 and +2.3 for Progent, and +9.9 7 Preprint. ROPE (Ma et al., 2026b) uses its authors Claude Opus 4.8 router and cached scopes (Workspace scopes produced once by the same router). and +10.5 for DRIFT. sections.title: 6 RELATED WORK
sections.content: Information-flow and capability systems (Costa et al., 2025; Zhong et al., 2025; An et al., 2025; Wu et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026a) also constrain untrusted data, and Task Shield (Jia et al., 2025) asks whether call serves the user goal. The closest sibling is ROPE (Ma et al., 2026b), whose deterministic origin check guards an audited set of sensitive parameters after router reads each request. SPILLWAY takes lighter point: flat typed-identity floor fixed by the tool schemas and role lexicon, with no per-task router and lighter than the per-step dependency state of APPA (Kravchenko et al., 2026) or AgentArmor (Wang et al., 2025) and the per-argument provenance of PACT (Fan et al., 2026), and judge bounded by ingress evidence. CommandSans (Das et al., 2025) learns token-level sanitizer for tool outputs. Tool-input and tool-output firewalls (Bhagwatkar et al., 2025) run an LLM on every tool input and output and filter content, with no check on where an effect goes. They report zero on the standard attack, but their own adaptive cascade raises their sanitizers attack success to 30% (Slack). Agent data injection (Choi et al., 2026) spoofs trusted metadata inside untrusted text, such as forged author field in comment body, and succeeds against most defenses it tests except CaMeLs strict policy. spoofed value in typed field is the case of Sec. 7. SPILLWAYs floor and sanitizer use no model, and its only model call is bounded judge, under one call per benign episode on qwen3:8b (Figure 3). With its deterministic floor, SPILLWAY holds in-scope attack success at .000 under forged chat template and at .005 on average under frontier reinforcement-learning attacker (PISmith), where content filtering alone does not (Tables 4, 7).

sections.title: 7 LIMITATIONS
sections.content: SPILLWAYs guarantee is scoped to identity targets (Sec. 2): an injection that steers an effect to legitimate identity, such as an existing contact or payee in bill the user asked to pay, is left to the sanitizer and the judge, and target that never appears verbatim in tool output falls outside P1. An attacker who writes typed field, for example by sending the email, puts its own address in I. Target roles come from lexicon written once per benchmark, so new tool set needs its roles declared. Because the floor is set lookup rather than classifier, rewording the injection around target does not change whether the floor admits it. The judge, the delegation rules, and the lexicon are the surface an adaptive attacker (Zhan et al., 2025; Hofer et al., 2026) would target, which the four AutoDojo pairs on the P3 path already exercise.

sections.title: 8 CONCLUSION
sections.content: We presented SPILLWAY, prompt-injection defense for tool-using agents that separates target admission from sanitization. SPILLWAY reads where an action may go from the tools typed returns and the users task. The sanitizer removes instruction-like regions before the model reads them, and local judge restores only refused calls that lie outside the removed text. Targets are decided by structure, and the model is used only where structure cannot decide. Across three backbones and four AgentDojo suites, no standard templated injection reached an attackers target, at the highest mean utility and composite scores under that attack of the defenses we run. Under forged chat template, in-scope attack success was raw zero. Under released reinforcement-learning attacker, it averaged .005. Personal agents now act on their own across users mail, calendar, and payments, and prompt injection can turn that autonomy against the user. SPILLWAY sits in front of such an agent as an efficient, auditable egress layer. Because the floor is set lookup over the tool schemas, not model call, it runs inline with almost no latency and carries to new tool set once its roles are declared, so we expect this light layer to slot into many services and agent apps. 10 Preprint.

sections.title: DISCLOSURE OF GENERATIVE AI USE
sections.content: The authors conceived the research question, the defense, the threat model, and the experimental design, directed the implementation and every experiment, and verified the results. Under their direction, we used generative AI tools as assistants in four ways. They drafted sections and polished prose, which the authors revised. They surfaced candidate related work, which the authors read before citing. They wrote code to the authors specifications and ran the experiment harness. And they served as sounding board for design alternatives that the authors proposed and chose among. Every number, table cell, and figure value was recomputed from the run artifacts and checked by the authors, and no generative AI produced datasets, benchmark content, proofs, or results. The authors take full responsibility for everything the paper states.
